thread.title_full: WSU Program Gives Veterinary Students Hands-On Experience in Livestock Medicine - NewsBreak

author: Dailyfly Staff
title: WSU Program Gives Veterinary Students Hands-On Experience in Livestock Medicine - NewsBreak
text:
By Dailyfly Staff ,
9 hours ago PULLMAN, WA – A six-week paid summer externship is introducing Washington State University veterinary students to careers in livestock by pairing them with dairy and feedlot operations throughout the Pacific Northwest.
The WSU College of Veterinary Medicine’s Northwest Bovine Experience aims to increase the number of students interested in food animal medicine and expose them to the realities of the field. The decades-old program is especially critical amid a well-documented food animal veterinarian shortage in Washington state .
“This is really a special program and the goal is to provide an immersive veterinary experience and encourage students to pursue careers in food animal medicine,” said Dr. Lauren Christensen, a veterinarian who oversees the program as part of WSU’s partnership with the University of Idaho.
That immersive experience is exactly what drew fourth-year veterinary student Jordan Johnson to the program.
“It’s hard to find bovine-only experience in veterinary school, and this, for me, was invaluable in the sense that, for the first time, I could get a day-to-day vision of what bovine practice looks like and have the ability to live it for six weeks,” Johnson said.
Johnson completed her externship at Crazy Mountain Veterinary Service in White Sulfur Springs and Harlowton, Montana — a six-doctor , women-owned and -operated practice serving a large rural region. Johnson traveled extensively with veterinarians as they serviced ranches and producers across the state.
This gave me the ability to really see the lifestyle, the relationships with producers, and what the work actually looks like over time.
Jordan Johnson, student
Washington State University
“We were driving three hours one way some days,” Johnson said. “This gave me the ability to really see the lifestyle, the relationships with producers, and what the work actually looks like over time.”
The clinic’s caseload consisted primarily of large animal medicine, though Johnson also gained exposure to small animal care and emergency cases. During the externship, she assisted with breeding soundness exams and bull fertility testing, including semen collection and analysis, pregnancy checking, and routine herd work. She also scrubbed into surgeries and assisted with emergencies ranging from porcupine quill removals to casting broken legs in calves and horses.
For Johnson, who hopes to return to her home state of Wyoming to practice bovine medicine, the externship provided something difficult to replicate in a classroom setting: sustained immersion in food animal practice.
Since students spend six weeks embedded within a clinic, the program also allows them to progressively take on more responsibility and build meaningful relationships with veterinarians and producers alike.
“By week one they’re teaching you how everything works, and then by weeks three and four you’re able to really grow and participate more hands-on ,” Johnson said.
The paid externship and provided housing also help remove financial barriers for students pursuing food-animal experiences during the summer months.
“This was the first big paycheck I’d gotten as a veterinary student,” Johnson said. “Having housing provided and being paid to learn made a huge difference.”
Johnson said one of the most impactful parts of her experience was seeing a successful bovine practice that also prioritized work-life balance — something she believes is often overlooked in large animal medicine.
“They really illustrated that you can have a successful practice while still having an involved life outside of work,” Johnson said. “That was something I appreciated seeing because it’s not always what people expect from large animal practice.”
Looking back, Johnson said she only has one regret about the Northwest Bovine Experience.
“My only regret is that I only did it one summer,” she said. “This was one of the most important things I’ve done while I’ve been in veterinary school, especially as somebody who wants to go into bovine practice.”
